method: S1 (RACGP AJGP, October 2025) and S2 (Australian Prescriber 2017) are OPEN and checked verbatim (35 claims, 4 of them doses). A1 is AMH, read under subscription and PARAPHRASED (26 claims, 3 doses), no passage reproduced and no source_text stored. S1 and A1 give the SAME first-line eradication regimen; that agreement is stated rather than assumed, and S1's version carries a verbatim quote so the regimen is machine re-checkable here even though AMH's is not. Where they differ -- AMH permits a 7-day course if local clarithromycin resistance is low, S1 reports Cochrane favouring 14 days and rising Australian clarithromycin resistance -- both are stated and attributed. AP 2017 names ranitidine 300 mg twice daily; rather than assume that drug had been withdrawn, AMH's current H2 antagonist monograph was retrieved and still lists ranitidine, and that check is recorded instead of an assumption.

claims.claim: In Australia a pooled meta-analysis reported general population prevalence of H. pylori in adults of 24.8%, with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and Asian communities disproportionately represented with prevalence as high as 50 to 80%
claims.source_text: In Australia, a pooled meta-analysis reported the general population prevalence for adults was 24.8% (95% [confidence interval; CI], 21.7-55.9), with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and Asian communities disproportionately represented with prevalence as high as 50-80%.

claims.claim: Although most patients with H. pylori remain asymptomatic, nearly all will develop chronic gastritis, and early detection and eradication remains vital to preventing complications
claims.source_text: Although most patients with H. pylori remain asymptomatic, nearly all will develop chronic gastritis. Chronic gastritis can further progress to several severe complications with varying lifetime risk rates (Table 1). Early detection and eradication of H. pylori remains vital to preventing these complications and reducing individual disease burden.

claims.claim: S1 gives the lifetime risk of complications of H. pylori infection as peptic ulcer disease 10%, gastric adenocarcinoma 1 to 3% and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma under 0.1%
claims.source_text: Peptic ulcer disease 10 Gastric adenocarcinoma 1-3 Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma <0.1

claims.claim: The non-invasive test of choice for diagnosing H. pylori is a urea breath test, but preparation is required before undertaking it
claims.source_text: The non-invasive test of choice in diagnosing H. pylori is a UBT; however, preparation is required before undertaking the test

claims.claim: S1 gives urea breath test washout durations as 4 weeks for antibiotics and bismuth compounds, 2 weeks for cytoprotective agents such as sucralfate, 2 weeks for proton pump inhibitors, and the fasting period only for H2 antagonists and antacids
claims.source_text: - Antibiotics and bismuth compounds - Cytoprotective agents (sucralfate) - Proton pump inhibitors - H2 antagonists and antacids - 4 weeks - 2 weeks - 2 weeks - Fasting period only

claims.claim: All antibiotics, cytoprotective agents and proton pump inhibitors must be ceased before urea breath testing as they can cause false negative results
claims.source_text: Must cease all antibiotics, cytoprotective agents and proton pump inhibitors prior to testing as they can cause false negative results

claims.claim: Urea breath test sensitivity and specificity decrease significantly in paediatric populations, and a monoclonal stool antigen test is an acceptable alternative in adults and is preferred in paediatric patients because of increased sensitivity and specificity
claims.source_text: Sensitivity and specificity in paediatric populations significantly decreases when a urea breath test is conducted … A monoclonal stool antigen test is an acceptable alternative to a urea breath test in adults and is preferred in paediatric patients because of increased sensitivity and specificity (96.6-98.0% and 94.1-100%, respectively)

claims.claim: Serological tests might be considered as an alternative for diagnosis in adults unable to cease antibiotics, cytoprotective agents or proton pump inhibitors, with sensitivity 55.6 to 85% and specificity 79%
claims.source_text: Serological tests might be considered as an alternative in adults who are unable to cease antibiotics, cytoprotective agents or proton pump inhibitors (sensitivity and specificity 55.6-85% and 79%, respectively)

claims.claim: Clarithromycin-based triple therapy is the initial treatment of choice for H. pylori eradication, and a Cochrane review found extending treatment duration to 14 days significantly increased the eradication rate compared to a seven-day regimen
claims.source_text: Clarithromycin-based triple therapy is the initial treatment of choice for H. pylori eradication (Table 3). 5 A Cochrane review found extending the treatment duration to 14 days signiﬁcantly increased the eradication rate compared to a seven-day regimen.

claims.claim: S1 states that the 14-day duration presents logistical and financial challenges because the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme permits a single prescription without repeats, and recommends a follow-up review at seven days to consider the need for an additional prescription giving a total of 14 days
claims.source_text: This presents logistical and financial challenges for patients, as the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme permits a single prescription without repeats. A follow-up review at seven days is recommended to consider the need for an additional prescription, providing a total treatment duration of 14 days.

claims.claim: S1 gives standard first-line H. pylori therapy as esomeprazole 20 mg twice daily, clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily and amoxicillin 1 g twice daily for 14 days
claims.source_text: Esomeprazole 20 mg twice daily 14 days Clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily Amoxicillin 1 g twice daily

claims.claim: S1 gives first-line H. pylori therapy for patients with penicillin allergy as esomeprazole 20 mg twice daily, clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily and metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days
claims.source_text: First-line therapy for patients with a penicillin allergy (dose and duration) Esomeprazole 20 mg twice daily 14 days Clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily

claims.claim: A repeat urea breath test is recommended as a test of cure at least four weeks after completion of therapy
claims.source_text: A repeat UBT is recommended as a test of cure at least four weeks after completion of therapy to evaluate the eﬀectiveness of eradication therapy.

claims.claim: Red flag indications for urgent endoscopy referral are unexplained iron deficiency anaemia, unintentional weight loss with gastrointestinal symptoms, dysphagia or odynophagia, gastrointestinal bleeding and persistent vomiting
claims.source_text: - Unexplained iron deﬁciency anaemia - Unintentional weight loss with gastrointestinal symptoms - Dysphagia or odynophagia - Gastrointestinal bleeding - Persistent vomiting

claims.claim: Other indications for endoscopy referral are treatment failure, new symptoms in people aged over 50 years, severe or frequent symptoms, and changing or atypical symptoms
claims.source_text: Other indications - Treatment failure - New symptoms in people aged >50 years - Severe or frequent symptoms - Changing or atypical symptoms

claims.claim: In Australia treatment failure for H. pylori is primarily caused by poor adherence and increasing clarithromycin resistance
claims.source_text: In Australia, treatment failure for H. pylori is primarily caused by poor adherence and increasing clarithromycin resistance.

claims.claim: The most common side effects of H. pylori therapy are diarrhoea, altered taste and gastrointestinal upset, and it is recommended to assess side effects and monitor adherence at the seven-day review to support antibiotic completion and promote antimicrobial stewardship
claims.source_text: The most common side eﬀects of H. pylori therapy are diarrhoea, altered taste and gastrointestinal upset (Table 5). 8 It is recommended to assess side effects and monitor adherence at the seven-day review to support antibiotic completion and promote antimicrobial stewardship.

claims.claim: Previous use of proton pump inhibitors and macrolides is associated with increased rates of H. pylori treatment failure, and there is a positive association between smoking and treatment failure as well as an increased risk of gastric cancer with concurrent H. pylori infection
claims.source_text: Previous use of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and macrolides are also associated with increased rates of treatment failure, emphasising the need to prescribe according to the guidelines. 9,10 There is a positive association with smoking and treatment failure, in addition to an increased risk of developing gastric cancer with a concurrent H. pylori infection.

claims.claim: Family members with upper gastrointestinal symptoms or a positive family history of gastric cancer should be offered screening, treatment and follow-up to reduce the risk of progression
claims.source_text: Family members with upper gastrointestinal symptoms or a positive family history of gastric cancer should be offered screening, treatment and follow-up to reduce the risk of progression.

claims.claim: Patients with refractory H. pylori should avoid repeat eradication with first-line clarithromycin-based triple therapy because of low repeat success rates and the potential for further resistance, and clarithromycin resistance has significantly increased over the last 20 years in Australia
claims.source_text: Patients with refractory H. pylori should avoid repeat eradication with ﬁrst-line clarithromycin-based triple therapy because of low repeat success rates and the potential for further resistance. 5 Clarithromycin resistance has signiﬁcantly increased over the last 20 years in Australia.

claims.claim: In refractory cases salvage therapies are either restricted or available through special access schemes and include levofloxacin, colloidal bismuth subcitrate and tetracycline, with rifabutin and moxifloxacin as alternative options, and patients should be referred to a specialist including for gastroscopy
claims.source_text: In refractory cases, the management includes various salvage therapies, which are either restricted or available through special access schemes; these include levoﬂoxacin, colloidal bismuth subcitrate and tetracycline, whereas rifabutin and moxiﬂoxacin are alternative options depending on the context. 5 In these cases, patients should be referred to a specialist for further management including gastroscopy.

claims.claim: Clarithromycin can cause QT prolongation and metronidazole has alcohol interactions that can cause headache, flushing, nausea and vomiting
claims.source_text: Clarithromycin - Altered taste - Diarrhoea - Gastrointestinal upset - QT prolongation Metronidazole - Metallic taste - Dyspepsia - Alcohol interactions can cause headache, ﬂushing, nausea and vomiting

claims.claim: A peptic ulcer is a defect in the upper gastrointestinal mucosa extending through the muscularis mucosa into deeper layers of the gut wall, and the two major risk factors are Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs
claims.source_text: A peptic ulcer is a defect in the upper gastrointestinal mucosa that extends through the muscularis mucosa into deeper layers of the gut wall. There are two major risk factors for peptic ulcer disease - Helicobacter pylori and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

claims.claim: NSAIDs exert their therapeutic effects by inhibiting COX-2, while the gastric and renal toxicities are related to inhibition of COX-1, and there is a spectrum of COX-1 and COX-2 inhibition across the class
claims.source_text: NSAIDs exert their therapeutic anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects by inhibiting COX-2. The gastric and renal toxicities of the drugs are related to inhibition of the COX-1 isoform. 4, 5 There is a spectrum of COX-1 and COX-2 inhibition across the class of NSAIDs.

claims.claim: Gastrointestinal toxicity with NSAIDs including low-dose aspirin is highest in patients with risk factors including age over 65 years, past history of peptic ulcer disease, heart disease, and co-prescription of antiplatelets, corticosteroids and anticoagulants, with higher NSAID doses increasing risk
claims.source_text: Gastrointestinal toxicity with NSAIDs, including low-dose aspirin, is highest in patients with risk factors. These include increased age (>65 years), past history of peptic ulcer disease, heart disease, and co-prescription of antiplatelets, corticosteroids and anticoagulants. In addition, using higher doses of NSAIDs leads to an increased risk of upper gastrointestinal complications.

claims.claim: In chronic NSAID users with no risk factors only 0.4% have serious adverse events, but the risk is as high as 9% in patients with multiple risk factors
claims.source_text: In patients who are chronic users of NSAIDs and who have no risk factors, only 0.4% have serious adverse events. However, the risk is as high as 9% in patients with multiple risk factors.

claims.claim: S2 reports the relative risk of upper gastrointestinal complications as low under 2 for aceclofenac, celecoxib and ibuprofen, intermediate 2 to 4 for diclofenac, meloxicam and ketoprofen, higher 4 to 5 for naproxen, indomethacin and diflunisal, and highest for piroxicam at 7.4 and ketorolac at 11.5
claims.source_text: The relative risk of upper gastrointestinal complications for aceclofenac, celecoxib and ibuprofen is low (<2). Diclofenac, meloxicam and ketoprofen are intermediate (2-4) while naproxen, indomethacin and diflunisal have a higher relative risk (4-5). The highest pooled relative risk is associated with piroxicam (7.4) and ketorolac (11.5).

claims.claim: COX-2 inhibitors are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular events, and to avoid possible cardiovascular complications NSAIDs should be used at the lowest possible dose and for the shortest time
claims.source_text: However, COX-2 inhibitors are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular events. … However, to avoid possible cardiovascular complications the use of NSAIDs should be at the lowest possible dose and for the shortest time.

claims.claim: A meta-analysis of randomised trials of 57,000 patients taking low-dose aspirin revealed a relative risk of 2 for significant gastrointestinal adverse events such as bleeding, and in patients with a history of ulcer bleeding consideration needs to be given to secondary ulcer prevention with proton pump inhibitor therapy while changing aspirin to other antiplatelet therapy is not recommended
claims.source_text: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of 57 000 patients taking low-dose aspirin revealed a relative risk of 2 for significant gastrointestinal adverse events such as bleeding. 10 In patients with a history of ulcer bleeding consideration needs to be given to secondary ulcer prevention with proton pump inhibitor therapy. Changing aspirin to other antiplatelet therapy is not recommended.

claims.claim: A meta-analysis found selective COX-2 inhibitors combined with proton pump inhibitors had the lowest absolute event probability for ulcer complications, followed by a selective COX-2 inhibitor alone and a non-selective NSAID combined with a proton pump inhibitor, with all three strategies well tolerated
claims.source_text: It found that selective COX-2 inhibitors in combination with proton pump inhibitors were associated with the lowest absolute event probability for ulcer complications (0.07; 95% confidence interval 0.02-0.18). 13 This strategy may be the most effective way to reduce the risk of ulcer complications, followed by the use of a selective COX-2 inhibitor alone and a non-selective NSAID combined with a proton pump inhibitor. Importantly all three strategies were well tolerated by patients.

claims.claim: Proton pump inhibitors are slightly better at preventing duodenal ulcers than gastric ulcers and have assumed therapeutic dominance for minimising the gastrointestinal risks of NSAIDs due to their acceptable adverse effect profile
claims.source_text: Proton pump inhibitors are slightly better at preventing duodenal ulcers than gastric ulcers. … Due to their acceptable adverse effect profile, proton pump inhibitors have assumed therapeutic dominance for minimising the gastrointestinal risks of NSAIDs.

claims.claim: Pooled data showed that a single daily dose of an H2-receptor antagonist does not protect against NSAID-related gastric ulcers, but double doses of at least ranitidine 300 mg twice daily were effective in preventing gastric and duodenal ulcers compared to placebo
claims.source_text: However, the pooled data analysis showed that a single daily dose does not protect against NSAID-related gastric ulcers, but double doses of H 2 -receptor antagonist (at least ranitidine 300 mg twice daily) were effective in preventing gastric and duodenal ulcers when compared to placebo.

claims.claim: Misoprostol was effective in preventing gastric ulcers in 74% and duodenal ulcers in 53% compared with placebo, but its clinical usefulness is limited largely by gastrointestinal adverse effects such as cramping, abdominal pain and diarrhoea, making it a third-line drug option
claims.source_text: A large pooled data analysis showed misoprostol was effective in preventing gastric (74%) and duodenal ulcers (53%) in comparison with placebo. 10 Unfortunately, the clinical usefulness of the misoprostol is limited largely by its gastrointestinal adverse effects such as cramping, abdominal pain and diarrhoea, making it a third-line drug option.

claims.claim: Testing for H. pylori for ulcer prevention in asymptomatic patients should be assessed case by case and is not routinely recommended, but testing and eradicating is recommended in patients with a past history of peptic ulcer disease before starting low-dose aspirin or NSAIDs
claims.source_text: Testing for H. pylori for ulcer prevention in asymptomatic patients needs to be assessed on a case-by-case basis and is not routinely recommended. However, testing and eradicating H. pylori is recommended in patients with a past history of peptic ulcer disease before starting low-dose aspirin or NSAIDs.

claims.claim: Before prescribing an NSAID, prophylactic proton pump inhibitor therapy needs to be offered to patients with a past history of peptic ulcer disease and those on dual antiplatelet therapy or anticoagulant therapy
claims.source_text: Before prescribing an NSAID, prophylactic proton pump inhibitor therapy needs to be offered to patients with a past history of peptic ulcer disease and those on dual antiplatelet therapy or anticoagulant therapy.

claims.claim: AMH lists famotidine, nizatidine and ranitidine as H2 antagonists, which competitively block H2 receptors on parietal cells to reduce gastric acid secretion and are indicated for peptic ulcer disease, GORD and dyspepsia

claims.claim: H2 antagonists are generally well tolerated, may accumulate in renal impairment requiring dose reduction, should be continued throughout the perioperative period, and famotidine and ranitidine are safe in pregnancy with all safe in breastfeeding
claims.locator: AMH Medicines, drug class monograph 'H2 antagonists' at https://amhonline.amh.net.au/chapters/gastrointestinal-drugs/drugs-dyspepsia-reflux-peptic-ulcers/h2-antagonists, July 2026 release, read under subscription 2026-09-22
